aldemar.headline: The banks split and the tape froze — and the long end eased a third time before the print that settles it
aldemar.standfirst: Nothing on the board moved more than six tenths of a sigma, and the S&P closed 1.79 points lower at 7,805.45 after moving 4.30 on Monday. themes.note: September CPI has to settle three arguments that have run all fortnight. Whether the ISM prices indices at 77.9 and 74.0 are feeding through or stalling at the factory gate, when core PCE came in at 3.0% against 3.3% expected. Whether the Fed's minutes and Waller's comments describe a committee that will hike again or one that is talking, with the market at roughly a 78% hold for 28 October. And whether the long end is inflation or supply — where the evidence against the supply story is now three consecutive sessions, none of them driven by a release. Watch the energy line: gasoline was up 27.4% year-on-year in the last published report and crude has not come down since.

The term-premium story — that the long end is rising because of supply and global debt rather than inflation — has now been contradicted three times in a row, and not once by a release. That matters because the release arrives Wednesday: a hot print washes all three sessions away, and a soft one leaves the supply story needing to explain why yields fell on no news at all.

The Dow gave back the most, after leading for a week. JPMorgan missed for the first time in nearly three years, and the reason is the one that matters. $15.3bn, or $5.57 a share, against $5.93 expected — up from $5.07 a year ago, so this is a miss against expectations and not a fall in profit. Investment banking and a fixed-income desk that slowed from the summer did it. Set that against Goldman Sachs at $17.01 a share against $12.25 a year ago, driven by stock trading with bond trading slower, and the same fact appears twice: equities desks are busy and bond desks are not. In a quarter when the long end was supposed to be the story, the desks that trade the long end went quiet. Jamie Dimon's own framing was strong business investment and ongoing consumer spending on the surface, with sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates shifting underneath.

2. The Treasury fined Bank of America $1.2bn the same morning — the third-largest penalty in its history. FinCEN assessed it for failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, tied to Chinese money-laundering networks and illicit finance on the southwest border, with the bank admitting it willfully violated the 1970 Bank Secrecy Act; OFAC added an $11.6m settlement over apparent violations of sanctions programmes covering Iran, Russia, narcotics and terrorism. $750m of it goes to the Comptroller of the Currency, that agency's largest fine ever. Only the roughly $4bn Binance settlement of 2023 and the $3bn TD Bank settlement the year after are bigger. The bank's response was that financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right. A sector reporting record desk revenue and a record compliance penalty in the same four hours is the cleanest picture of this cycle anyone has published.

3. The consumer evidence came from outside the banks, and it was not reassuring. Citigroup's card profits were flat — the one direct read on the consumer in the whole batch, and it showed nothing. Meanwhile Kroger told staff it will cut about 3,000 corporate jobs over three years, roughly 37% of a corporate workforce of 8,200 and among the largest cuts in the company's 143-year history. Put that beside the labour contradiction already on file — payrolls at 29,000 against 90,000 expected with 60,000 revised away, against initial claims near a 57-year low — and the shape is consistent: almost nobody is being laid off from the jobs that exist, and the white-collar jobs are being removed structurally rather than cyclically. Neither of those shows up in a claims number.

The two benchmarks moved in opposite directions, and the reason is a diesel deal

WTI settled $94.14, up 40 cents or 0.43%. Brent settled $105.69, down 96 cents or 0.90%. The spread between them narrowed to about $11.55 from $12.91 in one session. Two benchmarks for the same commodity diverging on the same day means the news was about supply reaching a particular place, not about the world running short — and the news was that traders are weighing a United States–Russia deal on diesel fuel that would put more Russian supply into the market.

Against that, the conflict widened. Houthi forces said Saudi Arabia had attacked Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts. That is a second front operating on the same price: Monday's move came from Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, and Tuesday's came from Yemen and from a diesel negotiation. The market is now pricing at least four separate sources of interruption, which is why a three-percent day can be followed by a flat one without anything being resolved.

The structural position has not changed and it is worth restating once. Regional flow is back at pre-conflict rates — Kpler had exports above those levels on 14 days in September, a seven-day average of 18.3m barrels a day — while Aramco's Amin Nasser puts commercial inventory under 6 billion barrels against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, with less than 10% practically available and up to two years to rebuild. Full tanks would absorb a diesel deal and a Yemeni escalation without moving the price. Empty ones mean every one of these headlines prints.

What it means for this book, which is nothing direct and something indirect. Nothing here is positioned for oil and nothing needs to be. But crude at $94, with gasoline up 27.4% year-on-year in the last published CPI, is why the energy line is the first place to look in Wednesday's print for a hot number. The oil price is not a position in this book; it is an input to the only thing that can reprice all four of them at once.

Three index records were set this week and the only index that fell was the one measuring the median company. The Russell lost 0.91% — 2.12σ, the largest reading on the board — while the S&P rose 1.15% at 1.69σ, the Dow 0.93% and the Nasdaq 0.64% at 1.01σ. In point terms: S&P +88.82, Dow +477.99, Nasdaq +175.31, Russell −25.91. A record-setting week in which small caps fell is not a rally with poor breadth; it is two different markets, and this is the third consecutive week the gap has widened.

The rotation inverted, and the week is the evidence. The Dow beat the Nasdaq over the five sessions — 0.93% against 0.64% — after a quarter in which the Nasdaq beat the Dow by more than five points. The Dow led on three of the last four sessions. That is not a one-day funding effect any more. For a book holding three long-duration growth names and nothing on the other side, it is the single most relevant structural fact of the week, and it sits oddly beside the book's own result.

The rate story turned two-sided for the first time. Monday through Wednesday it ran exactly as it had for a fortnight: ISM services prices paid up 1.4 to 74.0 against 72.9 expected, a second month above 72, while employment sat at 50.1; the two-year falling on the weak half and the ten-year making 52-week highs at 5.315% and touching 5.35% intraday, the thirty-year at 5.670%. Wednesday added the global framing — France's index down 1.2% amid mass budget protests, debt heading for 121.7% of GDP in 2027, and projected interest payments of €74.5bn exceeding what the country spends on education. The IMF's Georgieva cited record public debt; Ray Dalio warned about America's.

Then it stopped behaving. Thursday the long end eased through a thirty-year auction — the first direct test of the supply argument, and the ten-year closed near 5.24%, its lowest in a week. Friday the curve flattened: the two-year rose 3.9 basis points to 4.795% while the thirty-year sat flat at 5.608%, and it did so on a Michigan sentiment print that fell to 46.3 from 48.1 against 47.6 expected. Two consecutive sessions now fail to fit the term-premium story after five that fitted it exactly. It is not refuted — the thirty-year is still near a 24-year high and the September Fed minutes promise another hike this year — but this is the first sustained counter-evidence, and CPI on Tuesday decides it.

And the week ended with a structural repricing nobody had on the calendar. A reported $8bn SpaceX purchase of 800 MHz spectrum for Starlink Mobile took 12.26% out of T-Mobile on Friday and about 10.9% each out of Verizon and AT&T, while Crown Castle rose 11.27% and the other tower owners with it. Eight sessions to recover nine dollars and one to lose four of them. Order-cut reports are a supply-chain read and are frequently wrong, but they are the first hard, checkable claim about the cycle, and the answer comes on 29 October.

Two positions past the +1R threshold where a breakeven stop becomes arithmetically interesting — both flagged in the dailies, neither urgent. And a result that is entirely unrealised, in a book that has not been touched in twenty-two sessions. The honest summary of the week is that it was the best one in two months and that nothing in it was earned by a decision.

The rate thesis acquired its first counter-evidence, and the rotation inverted

1. Two sessions broke the pattern that five had built. From 29 September the long end rose on data that argued for lower yields four times in five sessions — a twelve-year low in consumer confidence, a downside core PCE miss at 3.0% against 3.3%, payrolls at 29,000 against 90,000 with 60,000 revised out, and Monday's ISM services. By Wednesday the thirty-year was at 5.671% and the ten-year had touched 5.35%, its highest since 2002, with the framing turning global. Then Thursday the long end eased through a thirty-year auction, and Friday the curve flattened on a weak sentiment print. An auction is where a supply thesis is actually tested, and that one did not go badly. This brief has published the supply argument for a fortnight; it is recording the counter-evidence with the same weight.

2. The index records and the median stock are describing different economies. The S&P set its first record since 13 August on Tuesday with genuinely broad internals — ten of eleven sectors, the equal-weight index matching the cap-weighted one, positive volume at 65.1% of NYSE turnover — and still only 24 new 52-week highs, with the McClellan Summation negative. By Friday the week showed the S&P up 1.2% and the Russell down 0.9%, and Michigan consumer sentiment had fallen to 46.3. Three records in a week when small caps fell and the consumer reached a multi-decade low of confidence is a market carried by its largest weights. This book owns three of those weights, which is why it had its largest weekly gain in three weeks.

3. The AI trade showed its first crack, and it was about funding. Thursday the Nasdaq fell 1.25% on a semiconductor sell-off while the Dow rose and most S&P constituents were higher — the first session in this run where the AI complex moved alone. The trigger was an Nvidia-backed Australian data-centre company failing to raise the support it had sought: a question about the capital behind capacity rather than about demand for compute, and the more dangerous of the two, because capacity already contracted has to be paid for regardless. Alphabet carries $195-205bn of guided capex and, since Tuesday, a twenty-year obligation for 3.6 gigawatts of power. It was the only holding to fall that day. By Friday the market had moved on; the question has not been answered.

The week the war stopped setting the price of oil

Crude ended the week where it started. WTI went $91.11 to $90.76, a move of less than four tenths of a percent across five sessions that contained a hurricane, a tanker attack and a presidential commitment on military timing. The range inside that was wide — $87.77 on Tuesday, almost $93 on Thursday — and Brent finished $103.35. A price that round-trips through that much news is a price that has stopped taking its direction from the conflict.

The most consequential thing said was about the calendar. On Thursday Trump said the United States will not attack Iran before the November midterm elections, citing productive diplomacy. It is the first dated commitment on timing since the conflict began and it removes, for roughly four weeks, the tail the oil price had been intermittently pricing. Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz happened the same day. Washington's reply to Tehran's seven-point proposal reached the cabinet through Qatari mediation on 30 September and neither side has disclosed its contents since.

What moved the price was weather and Saudi pricing. Hurricane Isaias shut in about a quarter of Gulf of Mexico output mid-week, with Chevron, Shell and BP evacuating platforms and Shell pulling off six; the premium came out on Friday as the path clarified. Against that, OPEC+ held quotas at the previous weekend and Saudi Arabia cut Arab Light for Asian buyers to $5 below benchmark, a six-year low, from a $2 discount, to take share as Gulf flows recovered. Kpler had regional exports above pre-conflict levels on 14 days in September, with a seven-day average of 18.3m barrels a day on the 30th.

And the man selling the oil spent Monday explaining that there is none spare. Aramco's Amin Nasser, at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London, called global stockpiles scarily thin: under 6 billion barrels of commercial inventory against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, less than 10% practically available, around 3 billion barrels of supply lost and over a billion drawn to cover it, with rebuilding at up to two years even after Hormuz fully reopens and an extra 2 million barrels a day needed for eighteen months. The flow has recovered and the buffer has not. That is why a storm moved crude 2.7% on Wednesday, and it is the asymmetry this book carries without being positioned for it.

Whether the Fed's minutes and Waller's more hikes will likely be needed describe a committee that will act or one that is talking. And whether the long end is an inflation trade or a supply one — because Thursday's auction and Friday's flattening are the first two pieces of evidence for the second reading being wrong, and a hot print removes them.

Then nothing from the companies for a fortnight. Alphabet reports 28 October on the same day the Fed decides, Apple the 29th, Palantir 2 November, Okta in early December. Three of this book's holdings report inside five sessions at the end of the month, immediately after a rate decision. Apple's print now has an order-cut report to answer, and Alphabet's lands into a funding scare rather than an enthusiasm.

Three things to watch through the gap. Whether the broker-driven re-ratings hold: two positions in this book gained more than five percent on upgrades alone, with nothing from either company, and that is the least durable kind of gain there is. Whether the Dow keeps beating the Nasdaq — it did over a full week and on three of four sessions, and this book owns nothing on that side. And whether the Russell can stop falling: down 0.9% in a week the S&P gained 1.2% is the clearest available statement that the records are not describing the median company.

The standing discipline. Heat is 3.00R against a 3.0R cap, so nothing on the screener is actionable whatever it returns. All 3 holdings are green, the nearest any came to a stop in five sessions was 8.7% on the week's lowest low, and 2 of them now sit above +1R. The market is now pricing at least four separate sources of interruption, which is why a three-percent day can be followed by a flat one without anything being resolved.

The structural position has not changed and it is worth restating once. Regional flow is back at pre-conflict rates — Kpler had exports above those levels on 14 days in September, a seven-day average of 18.3m barrels a day — while Aramco's Amin Nasser puts commercial inventory under 6 billion barrels against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, with less than 10% practically available and up to two years to rebuild. Full tanks would absorb a diesel deal and a Yemeni escalation without moving the price. Empty ones mean every one of these headlines prints.

What it means for this book, which is nothing direct and something indirect. Nothing here is positioned for oil and nothing needs to be. But crude at $94, with gasoline up 27.4% year-on-year in the last published CPI, is why the energy line is the first place to look in Wednesday's print for a hot number. The oil price is not a position in this book; it is an input to the only thing that can reprice all four of them at once.

Three index records were set this week and the only index that fell was the one measuring the median company. The Russell lost 0.91% — 2.12σ, the largest reading on the board — while the S&P rose 1.15% at 1.69σ, the Dow 0.93% and the Nasdaq 0.64% at 1.01σ. In point terms: S&P +88.82, Dow +477.99, Nasdaq +175.31, Russell −25.91. A record-setting week in which small caps fell is not a rally with poor breadth; it is two different markets, and this is the third consecutive week the gap has widened.

The rotation inverted, and the week is the evidence. The Dow beat the Nasdaq over the five sessions — 0.93% against 0.64% — after a quarter in which the Nasdaq beat the Dow by more than five points. The Dow led on three of the last four sessions. That is not a one-day funding effect any more. For a book holding three long-duration growth names and nothing on the other side, it is the single most relevant structural fact of the week, and it sits oddly beside the book's own result.

The rate story turned two-sided for the first time. Monday through Wednesday it ran exactly as it had for a fortnight: ISM services prices paid up 1.4 to 74.0 against 72.9 expected, a second month above 72, while employment sat at 50.1; the two-year falling on the weak half and the ten-year making 52-week highs at 5.315% and touching 5.35% intraday, the thirty-year at 5.670%. Wednesday added the global framing — France's index down 1.2% amid mass budget protests, debt heading for 121.7% of GDP in 2027, and projected interest payments of €74.5bn exceeding what the country spends on education. The IMF's Georgieva cited record public debt; Ray Dalio warned about America's.

Then it stopped behaving. Thursday the long end eased through a thirty-year auction — the first direct test of the supply argument, and the ten-year closed near 5.24%, its lowest in a week. Friday the curve flattened: the two-year rose 3.9 basis points to 4.795% while the thirty-year sat flat at 5.608%, and it did so on a Michigan sentiment print that fell to 46.3 from 48.1 against 47.6 expected. Two consecutive sessions now fail to fit the term-premium story after five that fitted it exactly. It is not refuted — the thirty-year is still near a 24-year high and the September Fed minutes promise another hike this year — but this is the first sustained counter-evidence, and CPI on Tuesday decides it.

And the week ended with a structural repricing nobody had on the calendar. A reported $8bn SpaceX purchase of 800 MHz spectrum for Starlink Mobile took 12.26% out of T-Mobile on Friday and about 10.9% each out of Verizon and AT&T, while Crown Castle rose 11.27% and the other tower owners with it. The rate thesis acquired its first counter-evidence, and the rotation inverted

1. Two sessions broke the pattern that five had built. From 29 September the long end rose on data that argued for lower yields four times in five sessions — a twelve-year low in consumer confidence, a downside core PCE miss at 3.0% against 3.3%, payrolls at 29,000 against 90,000 with 60,000 revised out, and Monday's ISM services. By Wednesday the thirty-year was at 5.671% and the ten-year had touched 5.35%, its highest since 2002, with the framing turning global. Then Thursday the long end eased through a thirty-year auction, and Friday the curve flattened on a weak sentiment print. An auction is where a supply thesis is actually tested, and that one did not go badly. This brief has published the supply argument for a fortnight; it is recording the counter-evidence with the same weight.

2. The index records and the median stock are describing different economies. The S&P set its first record since 13 August on Tuesday with genuinely broad internals — ten of eleven sectors, the equal-weight index matching the cap-weighted one, positive volume at 65.1% of NYSE turnover — and still only 24 new 52-week highs, with the McClellan Summation negative. By Friday the week showed the S&P up 1.2% and the Russell down 0.9%, and Michigan consumer sentiment had fallen to 46.3. Three records in a week when small caps fell and the consumer reached a multi-decade low of confidence is a market carried by its largest weights. This book owns three of those weights, which is why it had its largest weekly gain in three weeks.

3. The AI trade showed its first crack, and it was about funding. Thursday the Nasdaq fell 1.25% on a semiconductor sell-off while the Dow rose and most S&P constituents were higher — the first session in this run where the AI complex moved alone. The trigger was an Nvidia-backed Australian data-centre company failing to raise the support it had sought: a question about the capital behind capacity rather than about demand for compute, and the more dangerous of the two, because capacity already contracted has to be paid for regardless. Alphabet carries $195-205bn of guided capex and, since Tuesday, a twenty-year obligation for 3.6 gigawatts of power. It was the only holding to fall that day. By Friday the market had moved on; the question has not been answered.

The week the war stopped setting the price of oil

Crude ended the week where it started. WTI went $91.11 to $90.76, a move of less than four tenths of a percent across five sessions that contained a hurricane, a tanker attack and a presidential commitment on military timing. The range inside that was wide — $87.77 on Tuesday, almost $93 on Thursday — and Brent finished $103.35. A price that round-trips through that much news is a price that has stopped taking its direction from the conflict.

The most consequential thing said was about the calendar. On Thursday Trump said the United States will not attack Iran before the November midterm elections, citing productive diplomacy. It is the first dated commitment on timing since the conflict began and it removes, for roughly four weeks, the tail the oil price had been intermittently pricing. Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz happened the same day. Washington's reply to Tehran's seven-point proposal reached the cabinet through Qatari mediation on 30 September and neither side has disclosed its contents since.

What moved the price was weather and Saudi pricing. Hurricane Isaias shut in about a quarter of Gulf of Mexico output mid-week, with Chevron, Shell and BP evacuating platforms and Shell pulling off six; the premium came out on Friday as the path clarified. Against that, OPEC+ held quotas at the previous weekend and Saudi Arabia cut Arab Light for Asian buyers to $5 below benchmark, a six-year low, from a $2 discount, to take share as Gulf flows recovered. Kpler had regional exports above pre-conflict levels on 14 days in September, with a seven-day average of 18.3m barrels a day on the 30th.

And the man selling the oil spent Monday explaining that there is none spare. Aramco's Amin Nasser, at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London, called global stockpiles scarily thin: under 6 billion barrels of commercial inventory against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, less than 10% practically available, around 3 billion barrels of supply lost and over a billion drawn to cover it, with rebuilding at up to two years even after Hormuz fully reopens and an extra 2 million barrels a day needed for eighteen months. The flow has recovered and the buffer has not. That is why a storm moved crude 2.7% on Wednesday, and it is the asymmetry this book carries without being positioned for it.
